idiom_name: IO.select loop with an io -> callback registry (async/nio4r as the library form)
implementation_notes: Ruby's core offers only the demultiplexer: IO.select(read_ios, write_ios, error_ios, timeout) blocks until at least one of the given IO objects is ready and returns three arrays of ready objects, so the initiation dispatcher is yours - a hash from IO object to callback, a registration API, and a loop that calls select and dispatches. The library form is a dependency: socketry/async describes itself as an asynchronous event-driven reactor for Ruby, nio4r wraps epoll/kqueue in a selectable object, and since Ruby 3.0 Fiber.set_scheduler lets a scheduler drive blocking-style fiber code from such a loop. The GVL means one such loop can only use one core for Ruby code, so scaling is by process unless handlers are purely I/O-bound (waits that release the GVL overlap).
code_sketch:
handlers = {}                                     # io => handler (the registry)
handlers[server] = ->(io) { handlers[io.accept_nonblock] = ->(c) { echo(c) } }

loop do
  ready, = IO.select(handlers.keys)               # demultiplex readiness
  ready.each { |io| handlers[io].call(io) }       # dispatch to the registered handler
end
pitfalls: IO.select is select(2)-shaped: the descriptor set is bounded (FD_SETSIZE on platforms that use select) and rescanned on every call, so large handle counts need nio4r or async.
An exception raised inside a dispatched handler kills the loop unless it is rescued; there is no per-handler isolation, so every handler owns its rescue path and its cleanup.

A blocking or CPU-bound handler (a slow regexp, a synchronous driver) stalls every other connection because the GVL keeps other Ruby threads from running; only waits that release the GVL actually overlap.

Registering or deregistering from another thread while the loop sits in IO.select needs a wakeup - an IO.pipe or IO#wakeup registered in the same set - otherwise the change waits for the next unrelated event.
